Getting started with graphlearnR

Source: vignettes/graphlearnR.Rmd
graphlearnR.Rmd

graphlearnR is a framework for machine learning on graphs written in R on top of the torch package. Nothing in it calls Python. This article walks through one complete workflow: load a graph, split it, train a graph neural network, evaluate it, and predict. Later articles cover each step in depth.

library(graphlearnR)
library(torch)

LibTorch must be installed once with torch::install_torch(). Every code chunk in these articles runs only when it is available.

A first graph

Zachary’s karate club is a social network of 34 club members. The club split into two factions, which is the node label. dataset_karate() returns it as a graph_data object with one hot node identity features.

g <- dataset_karate()
g
#> <graph_data> undirected graph: 34 nodes, 156 edges (78 undirected pairs)
#>   node features [34 x 34]
#>   node labels: factor with 2 levels
summary(g)
#> Graph summary: 34 nodes, 156 edges (undirected)
#>   node features: 34, edge features: 0
#>   self loops: FALSE, duplicate edges: FALSE, isolated nodes: 0
#>   in degree:
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>   1.000   2.000   3.000   4.588   5.000  17.000 
#>   node label counts:
#> 
#>  Mr. Hi Officer 
#>      17      17

The graph is undirected. graphlearnR stores each undirected pair in both directions, so message passing sees both, and records which stored edges belong to the same pair in g$edge_pair. Node indices are 1-based everywhere, like the rest of R.

g$edge_index[, 1:6]
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5] [,6]
#> [1,]    1    2    1    3    1    4
#> [2,]    2    1    3    1    4    1
g$edge_pair[1:6]
#> [1] 1 1 2 2 3 3

Split the nodes

split_nodes() adds disjoint logical masks. With a factor label it stratifies by class, so each split keeps the class balance.

g <- split_nodes(g, train = 0.5, val = 0.25, test = 0.25, seed = 42)
table(train = g$train_mask, label = g$y)
#>        label
#> train   Mr. Hi Officer
#>   FALSE      8       8
#>   TRUE       9       9

Build and train a model

gnn_model() builds a stack of message passing layers. Here a two layer GraphSAGE network maps the 34 input features to 16 hidden units and then to two class scores.

torch_manual_seed(1)
model <- gnn_model("sage", input_dim = 34, hidden_dim = 16, output_dim = 2,
                   dropout = 0.3)
model
#> An `nn_module` containing 1,666 parameters.
#> 
#> ── Modules ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> • convs: <nn_module_list> #1,632 parameters
#> • head: <nn_linear> #34 parameters

train_graph_model() runs the training loop. The loss for node classification is cross entropy on the training nodes only; the validation nodes drive early stopping, and the best weights are restored at the end.

fit <- train_graph_model(model, g, task = "node_classification",
                         epochs = 150, lr = 0.01, weight_decay = 5e-4,
                         early_stopping = 20, seed = 1)
fit
#> <graph_fit> node_classification, 45 epochs on cpu
#>   final train loss 0.0022, val loss 0.4130, val accuracy 0.8750
#>   best epoch 25
tail(fit$history)
#>    epoch   train_loss  val_loss val_metric   lr seconds
#> 40    40 0.0028915016 0.3628182      0.875 0.01   0.022
#> 41    41 0.0004772095 0.3762871      0.875 0.01   0.022
#> 42    42 0.0017317395 0.3893111      0.875 0.01   0.023
#> 43    43 0.0035787998 0.3998920      0.875 0.01   0.027
#> 44    44 0.0023367275 0.4064358      0.875 0.01   0.021
#> 45    45 0.0022041511 0.4130065      0.875 0.01   0.020

Evaluate and predict

evaluate_graph_model() scores the held out test nodes.

evaluate_graph_model(fit, g)
#>              metric      value
#> 1          accuracy 1.00000000
#> 2 balanced_accuracy 1.00000000
#> 3   precision_macro 1.00000000
#> 4      recall_macro 1.00000000
#> 5          f1_macro 1.00000000
#> 6               ece 0.06625122
#> 7             brier 0.01589126
#> 8           roc_auc 1.00000000

predict() returns a data frame with one row per node, a predicted class, and a probability per class. Other types return only the classes, the probability matrix, the raw scores, or the node embeddings.

pred <- predict(fit, g)
head(pred)
#>   .row node_id .pred_class .prob_Mr. Hi .prob_Officer
#> 1    1       1      Mr. Hi    0.9587319    0.04126804
#> 2    2       2      Mr. Hi    0.9602939    0.03970613
#> 3    3       3      Mr. Hi    0.8446112    0.15538870
#> 4    4       4      Mr. Hi    0.9614742    0.03852574
#> 5    5       5      Mr. Hi    0.9683224    0.03167759
#> 6    6       6      Mr. Hi    0.9551980    0.04480197
emb <- predict(fit, g, type = "embedding")
dim(emb)
#> [1] 34 16
